elements.text:
This link masking surfaced a simple but important issue with the sieve, as it gets applied naturally to the header table, as it the keys are 23 bits and the header is word aligned (32 bits). This leaves 9 non-aligned bits for the sieve. Because this results in a 7 bit screen and a 2 bit selector, the number of screens is limited to 2^2, and saturates pretty quickly. The 16 screen point filter never saturates, so I never saw the issue, and it was subtle enough to not be caught in test.

When the sieve becomes "full" (last screen applied) the first bit of the sieve value must be zeroed. This corresponds to explicit mask of that sentinel bit in the mask table. If it is not masked it's possible for a full (not yet saturated) sieve to produce the empty sentinel, resulting in false negatives (which is bad). That's now resolved, and there is no impact to previous perf measurements.

elements.text: Also just made the secondary hash function (used by the sieve), independent of the primary in the case of non-point hashing (so like tx/block hashes and links). That was already complete for point hashing. This primarily advantages the header table, as it has a [[9][23]] bit split for [[sieve][link]], where the sieve is pointless if the hashes are not independent. Also made sure that both hashes stick to the lowest order bytes where possible, to avoid block hash zeros, and overlap minimally when the key space is limited.

I was thinking today about the bloom filtering estimation I did previously. I wasn't entirely happy with the estimates that I was getting from Grok, so I finally decided to just make an equivalent bloom implementation that could serve as a drop-in replacement for sieve. I just completed that, with a full test quite, and am now running the scenario with the same size filters on the tables, and reporting false positive rates for the point table. This will give me a block-by-block comparison.

Tuning is potentially a variable. I know that for Sieve LF=1.5, m=32 ... k=4 is optimal. Grok says that for Bloom LF=1.5, m=32 ... k=5 is optimal. The advantage of Bloom is that it doesn't store k values, so it can use all 32 bits for filtering (vs. 28 for Sieve in this example). I'll run Bloom at k=4 and k=6 just to make sure 5 is its optimum.

elements.text:
The redesign of filters split the filter head and filter body computations into the validate and confirm chasers.

When validating we have the data necessary to populate the filter body, which is the block and its populated previous outputs. These are hugely expensive to obtain, so we don't ever want to have to do it twice. If we aren't validating, but are filtering, then we just bypass the validation aspects in the chaser. Filter body creation is entirely independent of the filter header creation, and has the same ordering constraint as validation.

The result is written to an arraymap. This means there is no hashmap, just an array header which positions the link to the body element in the array element corresponding to the block surrogate key. Since blocks are keyed sequentially (by insert) there is no chance of a conflict, even if we happened to write the same block twice. That would just lead to two bodies and the last writer winning in the array head. This technique was developed to avoid using hashmaps for the prevout cache table.

Filter header creation hash the same ordering constraint as block confirmation. The previous filter header must exist to create the next. And of course the body must have been created (during validation). So confirmation reads out the body and the parent block filter header, computes the current header and writes it to the filter header arraymap. This table is also an arraymap because it's also block-aligned, and the indexing needs to be independent of the body table because of their independent creations along with the table append-only rule. But the heads for these are very small, so independent tables with no hashmap lookup is very efficient. Given that filer header creation must read from both the filter header and body tables, avoiding hashmaps in favor of arraymaps is a big savings.

So that's all done and checked in now. Sizing and perf numbers coming next.

elements.text: I should point out that writing the same block (by natural key) twice just creates two different instances, with their own links, one of which could get confirmed and end up typically being referenced for filter queries. This is extremely rare but possible and fine. I was referring to the other even more unlikely (probably impossible for the node to produce) but also fine (for the database) scenario of a filter for the same block instance (same surrogate key) being written to one or both of the arraymaps.

elements.text:
There has been one, long-standing, mysterious behavior in the node. You may have heard me talk of it in past meetings. It seemed to come and go randomly, unaffected by my attempts to isolate it, and narrowly focused around segwit txs. Specifically, witness data would be missing at script validation time (causing validation failure). It wasn't clear whether the data was supposed to be there or incorrectly expected, or whether it was read and lost, or never read, from either the wire or the store. But sparse reproduction and many possibilities made it very hard to diagnose.

So finally I put in diagnostics to trace out the segwit tx count for each block. Given that this count is driven off of witness data, this shows what I'm getting off the wire. Then when the validation failure occurred, I also wrote out the count. That was a couple weeks ago. Last night it happened again. The failing blocks were read from the wire without witness data, and all failed for lack of witness data, and were read from the store without witness data. So either there was an intermittent failure to read the data off the wire, or another mystery.

But given that there was just this isolated and contiguous segment of blocks with missing data it finally dawned on me what was happening. There is a peer that is sending non-segwit serializations despite negotiation for witness data serializations. This doesn't get caught by the witness commitment check, because it's optional without witness data. The requirement for witness data can only be determined by investigating the script patterns (which is what precipitates the later validation failure).

Fortunately most blocks above segwit have witness data, so this additional check is very rarely required - only when segwit is active and only for blocks with no witness data (which is already checked during the commitment validation). Without this the block gets archived and later during validation (and not at all during milestone) the scripts are validated - resulting in an invalidation of the archived block, and subsequent stall. This manifests similarly to a block hash malleability failure.

elements.text: So I've added the secondary check in the
block.check(context)

call, which will result in rejection of the block immediately after download, in the case where segwit is negotiated and required witness serialization is missing. And immediate dropping of the peer. Basically it just internally extends
block.is_invalid_witness_commitment()
with no interface changes.

There appears to have been an unexpected performance gain on the mini. I have not tried validating with a large window on the mini in a very long time. Normally I run 5k for validation on the mini, and 50k or higher for milestone. And always 50k or higher on the maxi. This is for data locality, as it improves query response and reduces paging. However the small window also reduces concurrency and can significantly slow milestone for example.

Well I accidentally ran a full validation on the mini with a 50k window AND the 100GB Electrum table population AND I had the validation tables set for milestone, so the was only 1 bucket in validate_bk, which turns this 1.7M entry table into a linked list! Nevertheless, the full validation run completed in well under 8 hours - breaking the record. This should mean that the filters could also be populated at the same time, with little impact, since most of that is just what's already available during validation. I'll have to spend some time isolating whether this was caused by the window size increase. But I think that the slew of changes over time made the narrow window less important.

If this holds up, we have full validation, with full ElectrumX index, full Compact Filters index, and the always-on full spender, tx, header, and height indexes - completing in under 8 hours on a $350 machine.

elements.text: I believe that the main reason I originally reduced the mini window to 5k was that it significantly improved the costly confirmation query due to improved data locality. However this query has been almost entirely eliminated. The larger window improves concurrency by reducing the gaps in the sawtooth pattern by 50/5 or 10x. That's significantly more time spent validating vs. waiting on blocks. The fastest runs are with an unlimited window, which in theory eliminates download gaps altogether. However when validating this can lead to arbitrarily long delays when waiting or an early block. 50k is therefore a good compromise when validating, otherwise unlimited. And it now looks like we no longer need to worry about varying the download window based on RAM/SSD size/speed.

elements.text: This is a consequence of recent optimizations in writing the
set_strong

table (confirmation records), and simplification of the organization process. I also resolved the potential data integrity issue with confirmation records - confirmation index becoming inconsistent with strong following a disk full pause/restart. I ended up using a two phase commit between these records. By ensuring they are both allocated before becoming written and accessible there is no risk of an inconsistency (publicly atomic).

elements.text: A huddle started

Generally speaking all of our tables are allocated, written, and then linked. Linkage is either from another table, or from the table head. We manage the creation of these records so that no element is accessible (linked) until it has been allocated and written. Given that head updates are atomic, this is fully thread safe. However I realized the two height indexes are never actually linked, they are just immediately public once allocated. This is problematic given that the write (of the header link) to the element follows the allocation. This can lead to a read conflicting with a write, resulting in an invalid read result.

elements.text: I resolved this by adding the ability to explicitly reserve elements, just as we do when we expand the tables, without this affecting the logical table size. This means the reservations guarantee space, but that space is not part of the logical array. The space is then written and the logical size updated. The increase in logical size is already atomic, so that results in a safe publication of the record. This was simple except it had a big impact on test mocks. That's now updated as well, and the issue is resolved without any additional locking or performance hit.
